topic.title: $10 million doing nothing out-earns a $500,000 salary

title: The $500,000 surgeon vs the $10 million heir 🤫
description:
Can $10 million that never goes to work out-earn a $500,000 salary?
One year: the surgeon works every shift; the heir's money sits invested at an assumed 7% a year, computed. Returns are assumptions, never promises. Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.
cta: Salary or money at work? Comment

lines.text: In an average year, my money out-earns a surgeon. And it never goes to work.
Wait, what? A top surgeon makes $500,000 a year!
Night shifts. Weekends. Every dollar earned with his own hands.
My $10,000,000 just sits invested, at an assumed 7% a year.
In an average year, it earns $700,000. I didn't lift a finger.
That's $200,000 more than the surgeon's whole salary.
So your money works harder than a surgeon? And what if it drops?
Some years it falls. Some years it jumps. I just never sell.
Every dollar you leave invested goes to work for you. That's why I say...

doctor beat: 'A doctor makes $500,000 a year!' is stated as a general fact in a global video; typical US physician pay is roughly $350-400K (and far lower in most countries), $500K is top-specialist pay. Make it 'this surgeon' / 'a top surgeon' or use a typical figure.

hook beat: toast 'Interest credited +$700,000' frames a 7% stock-market-style return as interest; no savings/deposit pays 7% in USD (ceiling ~5%). Label it as an assumed investment return (e.g. 'Assumed return'), not interest.

hook/earns beats: 'My money earns more than a doctor' and 'In a single year, it earns $700,000' present one year's 7% as certain; 7% is a long-run average assumption and a single year can be negative. Hedge the claim (e.g. 'in an average year', 'at that assumed 7%') so the comparison doesn't hide the risk.
